title.analysis: Authentic title "Why Is the World In So Much Debt" is a why-question frame. The script answers it (debt is money's plumbing, the rate changed rather than the pile) and resolves it with five historical exits rather than a collapse.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 17984 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored text is truncated mid-sentence ("...make sure that everything you own is earning more than"), so the final words are missing; the sister is rendered as Pria/Priya; garbles include "100red trillion", "4/10en", "fuel cues" and "doomframing"; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: You are at a closing table and the loan officer slides a sheet across to you. $400,000 house, $80,000 down, which took you 6 years, $320,000 borrowed. And the number at the bottom, the one you pay every month for 30 years, says $2,129. Your sister Pria bought the same floor plan two streets over in 2021. Same price, same down payment, same loan. Her payment is $1,349, $780 a month between you and your own sister for the same
script.ending_words: It is not free anymore. Nobody sent you a notice. The rate changed and everything built on top of it, including the number on the sheet in front of you, changed with it. You are not bad with money. The price of money moved while you were living your life. So find out what your rate actually is and then make sure that everything you own is earning more than
script.analysis: Full 17984 canonical characters read. A single-narrator explainer anchored on a mortgage-rate story (the viewer vs sister Priya): the $780 gap, global debt totals and per-person math, scale of a trillion, falling debt-to-GDP, bank money creation, saver Hector, US federal debt and the interest bill, refinancing mechanics, an emotional beat, a community promotion, who owns US debt, Japan, the Reinhart-Rogoff error, Britain 2022 and Sri Lanka, five exits, the rate floor under consumer credit, perspective on household debt, practical advice and an 1835 close. Arithmetic reproduces; most statistics are correct; the transcript is truncated at the end.
beat_map: Debt-to-GDP falling; rate is the story.
